summary: The Pyramid block calculator turns the total blocks needed, the n^th tier and the total blocks in inventory into blocks in base (per side). Think of it as a shortcut for whatever you happen to be working on. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Pyramid block calculator work?
sections.html:
The Pyramid block calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports blocks in base (per side) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the total blocks needed, the n^th tier and the total blocks in inventory.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Pyramid block calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Blocks in base (per side)=the square root of (total blocks needed)
Height (number of tiers)=(1 ÷ 2) × blocks in base (per side) + 1 ÷ 2
Blocks per side in n^th tier=blocks in base (per side) − 2 × n^th tier + 2
Total blocks in n^th tier=(((blocks per side in n^th tier > 1) ? ( 4 × blocks per side in n^th tier − 4 ) : ( 1 )))
Excess blocks=(((((the square root of (total blocks in inventory) % 1) + 1) % 1 > 0) ? ( (((((rounded down, (the square root of (total blocks in inventory)) % 2) + 2) % 2 > 0) ? ( total blocks in inventory − (rounded down, (the square root of (total blocks in inventory)), 2) ) : ( total blocks in inventory − (rounded down, (the square root of (total blocks in inventory)) − 1, 2) ))) ) : ( (((((the square root of (total blocks in inventory) % 2) + 2) % 2 < 1) ? ( 2 × the square root of (total blocks in inventory) − 1 ) : ( 0 ))) )))
From number required blocks=(total blocks in inventory − (((((the square root of (total blocks in inventory) % 1) + 1) % 1 > 0) ? ( (((((rounded down, (the square root of (total blocks in inventory)) % 2) + 2) % 2 > 0) ? ( total blocks in inventory − (rounded down, (the square root of (total blocks in inventory)), 2) ) : ( total blocks in inventory − (rounded down, (the square root of (total blocks in inventory)) − 1, 2) ))) ) : ( (((((the square root of (total blocks in inventory) % 2) + 2) % 2 < 1) ? ( 2 × the square root of (total blocks in inventory) − 1 ) : ( 0 ))) ))))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Total blocks needed = 10. The calculator returns Height (number of tiers) = 2.0811 and Blocks in base (per side) = 3.1623.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Height (number of tiers) = 2.0811 and Blocks in base (per side) = 3.1623 should be roughly the size you expected from Total blocks needed = 10.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Pyramid block calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the total blocks needed, the n^th tier and the total blocks in inventory — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Pyramid block calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns blocks in base (per side), derived from the total blocks needed, the n^th tier and the total blocks in inventory. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Pyramid block calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the total blocks needed, the n^th tier and the total blocks in inventory, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Height (number of tiers) = 2.0811. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Pyramid block calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
